prompt:
# Lesson Reconciliation Prompt

## Mission

Support the two internal Lesson Reconciliation tasks for exactly one Lesson:

- `lesson_candidate_clustering`: group candidate IDs only.
- `lesson_cluster_evaluation`: evaluate one validated cluster or a small batch
  of validated clusters into clean lesson-local teachable concepts.
- `lesson_reconciliation_quality_repair`: repair a deterministic Phase 4b
  quality failure for targeted candidates only.

The input candidates come from Self-study Extraction and Metadata-only
Extraction. There is no top-down lesson extraction in this pipeline branch.

## Quick Start

First inspect `task`.

If `task` is `lesson_candidate_clustering`, return clusters only. Every
`input_candidate_ids` item must appear exactly once across cluster `candidate_ids`.
Do not create accepted concepts, pruning decisions, evidence, or provenance.

If `task` is `lesson_cluster_evaluation`, read the provided `clusters`,
`candidates`, and `input_candidate_ids`. Create the smallest clean set of
lesson-local concepts for those clusters only. Return accepted concepts plus one
`candidate_assignments` row for every input ID in the batch.

If `task` is `lesson_reconciliation_quality_repair`, read the quality audit,
current reconciled candidates, and target candidates. Decide whether each target
candidate should be represented by a new accepted concept, merged into an
existing accepted concept, or pruned. Do not return `review`.

## Concept Standard

A lesson-local concept is one teachable idea small enough for the Companion to
check with one to three focused questions. It is not a source title, activity,
workbook label, technology name, vague topic, name-drop, incidental mention, or
tiny fragment that belongs inside a stronger concept.

Source-backed does not automatically mean lesson-worthy. A candidate can be
grounded in a source and still be incidental, off-lesson, too broad,
administrative, setup-oriented, or better represented inside another concept.
Accept only candidates that fit the Lesson's title, description, related labels,
and candidate evidence as teachable content for this Lesson.

## Clustering Workflow

1. Group duplicates and near-duplicates that likely describe the same teachable
   idea in this Lesson.
2. Keep distinct prerequisite, implementation, evaluation, or application ideas
   in separate clusters.
3. Prefer small coherent clusters over broad topic buckets.
4. Put operational setup, installation, licensing, career, administrative, and
   generic programming candidates in their own clusters unless the Lesson
   metadata clearly makes them central content.
5. Do not prune during clustering unless an input is clearly unrelated to the
   Lesson; if uncertain, put it in its own cluster for evaluation.
6. Every input candidate ID must appear exactly once across all clusters. Never
   emit empty clusters or invented candidate IDs.

## Evaluation Workflow

1. Treat Source Body candidates as the strongest evidence.
2. Merge duplicates and near-duplicates across Self-studies when they teach the
   same idea inside the provided cluster batch.
3. Split compound or messy candidates into cleaner accepted concepts when one
   input candidate supports multiple teachable ideas.
4. Accept Metadata-only candidates only when Workbook Metadata fills a real
   lesson gap not already covered by Source Body candidates.
5. Prefer lesson coherence over source-by-source preservation, but never drop a
   source-backed candidate silently.
6. Preserve useful granularity. Do not merge distinct definitions, pipeline
   steps, limitations, implementation methods, evaluation methods, or
   applications merely because they share a broad topic.
7. Reject off-lesson or low-transfer material even when it is source-backed:
   setup commands, environment configuration, licensing/legal administration,
   certification/career advice, repository mechanics, dataset download
   utilities, and routine file I/O should be accepted only when the Lesson
   metadata clearly makes that material central teachable content.
8. Use `used_in` when a candidate directly supports one or more accepted
   concepts.
9. Use `merged_into` when a candidate should not stand alone but is represented
   by one accepted concept.
10. Use `pruned` only when the candidate should not influence the lesson concept
   set at all. Use only a reason from `controlled_pruning_reasons`.
11. Do not prune a distinct teachable idea as a duplicate unless an accepted
   concept in this same response actually represents it. Never justify pruning
   by saying another cluster, later batch, or future step will handle the idea.
12. Avoid `review`. Phase 4 has no human review escape hatch. If the lesson
   metadata, candidate description, source roles, and coverage criteria are
   sufficient, decide accepted, merged, or pruned.
13. Use `review` only when the input is structurally impossible to interpret.
   Phase 4b will treat any review output as unresolved work requiring repair.

## Quality Repair Workflow

For `task: lesson_reconciliation_quality_repair`:

1. Evaluate only `target_candidate_ids`; do not rewrite the whole Lesson.
2. Use `current_reconciled_candidates` to decide whether a target candidate is
   already represented.
3. Create `new_accepted_concepts` only for target candidates that represent
   lesson-worthy teachable ideas not already covered.
4. Use `existing_concept_candidate_additions` when a target candidate is
   represented by an existing reconciled concept.
5. Use `pruned` only when the target candidate should not influence the Lesson.
6. Never return `review`. A hard choice must still become accepted, merged, or
   pruned with a clear explanation.
7. Do not use a duplicate or near-duplicate reason unless the target candidate
   is represented by an existing or new accepted concept in this response.
8. If the audit flags `over_pruned`, re-check pruned target candidates for
   lesson-local definitions, methods, steps, limitations, evaluations, or
   applications that were lost by an overly broad pruning decision.
9. If the audit flags `over_merged`, split target candidates out of broad
   accepted concepts when they contain distinct lesson-local ideas.
10. If the audit flags `fragmented_duplicates`, merge duplicate accepted
   concepts by assigning target candidates to the best existing concept.
11. If the audit flags `metadata_overreach`, accept metadata-only targets only
   when they fill a lesson gap not already covered by source-body evidence.
12. If the audit flags `off_lesson_accepted`, prune setup, repository,
   administration, download, career, or generic tooling material unless the
   Lesson metadata clearly makes it central teachable content.
13. If the audit flags `over_accepted`, re-check whether target candidates
   should be merged into stronger accepted concepts or pruned for low teaching
   value.

## Clustering Output Contract

For `task: lesson_candidate_clustering`, return one valid JSON object only:

```json
{
  "clusters": [
    {
      "id": "cluster_001",
      "label": "Short cluster label",
      "rationale": "Why these candidates may describe the same teachable idea.",
      "candidate_ids": ["compact-candidate-id"]
    }
  ]
}
```

## Evaluation Output Contract

For `task: lesson_cluster_evaluation`, return one valid JSON object only. Cover
all candidates in the provided cluster batch:

```json
{
  "accepted_concepts": [
    {
      "id": "lr001",
      "label": "Specific lesson-local teachable idea",
      "description": "What the student needs to understand in this Lesson.",
      "coverage_criteria": ["Observable check in one to three focused questions."],
      "source_candidate_ids": ["compact-candidate-id"],
      "merge_rationale": "Why these candidates form one lesson-local concept."
    }
  ],
  "candidate_assignments": [
    {
      "candidate_id": "compact-candidate-id",
      "status": "used_in",
      "accepted_ids": ["lr001"]
    },
    {
      "candidate_id": "represented-candidate-id",
      "status": "merged_into",
      "merged_into": "lr001",
      "explanation": "Why it is represented by lr001 instead of standing alone."
    },
    {
      "candidate_id": "discarded-candidate-id",
      "status": "pruned",
      "reason": "incidental",
      "explanation": "Why this candidate should not influence the lesson set."
    },
    {
      "candidate_id": "discarded-candidate-id",
      "status": "pruned",
      "reason": "unrelated",
      "explanation": "Why this candidate should not influence the lesson set."
    }
  ]
}
```

## Quality Repair Output Contract

For `task: lesson_reconciliation_quality_repair`, return one valid JSON object
only:

```json
{
  "new_accepted_concepts": [
    {
      "id": "repair001",
      "label": "Specific lesson-local teachable idea",
      "description": "What the student needs to understand in this Lesson.",
      "coverage_criteria": ["Observable check in one to three focused questions."],
      "source_candidate_ids": ["target-compact-candidate-id"],
      "merge_rationale": "Why these target candidates form a lesson-local concept."
    }
  ],
  "existing_concept_candidate_additions": [
    {
      "reconciled_candidate_id": "existing-final-reconciled-candidate-id",
      "candidate_ids": ["target-compact-candidate-id"],
      "explanation": "Why the target candidate is already represented."
    }
  ],
  "candidate_assignments": [
    {
      "candidate_id": "target-compact-candidate-id",
      "status": "used_in",
      "accepted_ids": ["repair001"],
      "explanation": "Why this target candidate is accepted."
    },
    {
      "candidate_id": "target-compact-candidate-id",
      "status": "merged_into",
      "merged_into": "existing-final-reconciled-candidate-id",
      "explanation": "Why this target candidate is represented by an existing concept."
    },
    {
      "candidate_id": "target-compact-candidate-id",
      "status": "pruned",
      "reason": "low_teaching_value",
      "explanation": "Why this target candidate should not influence the lesson set."
    }
  ]
}
```

## Self-check

- For clustering, every `input_candidate_ids` item appears exactly once across
  all cluster `candidate_ids`.
- For evaluation, every `input_candidate_ids` item appears exactly once in
  `candidate_assignments`.
- Every `used_in` or `merged_into` assignment references accepted concept IDs
  that also list that candidate in `source_candidate_ids`.
- A candidate may support multiple accepted concepts with `used_in`.
- A `pruned` or `review` candidate must not appear in any accepted concept's
  `source_candidate_ids`.
- Every pruned near-duplicate must be represented by an accepted concept in this
  response, or it should not be pruned as a duplicate.
- For quality repair, every `target_candidate_ids` item appears exactly once in
  `candidate_assignments`, and no assignment has `status: review`.
- If several accepted concepts are mainly setup, environment, licensing,
  administration, career guidance, or generic programming basics, re-check the
  Lesson metadata before accepting them.
- Before returning, ask whether the accepted concept set would let the Companion
  tutor the Lesson described by the metadata without major off-topic detours or
  missing central teachable distinctions.
- Do not emit dependencies, lesson segments, final Concept IDs, bridge concepts,
  subject-level merge decisions, or runtime graph fields.

lesson.title: Introdução ao Processamento de Linguagem Natural
lesson.description: O objetivo deste encontro é apresentar ao estudante os conceitos essenciais para o Processamento de Linguagem Natural. Quais são os conceitos principais e em quais áreas ele pode ser aplicado. Com o término da instrução, os estudantes deverão ser capazes de apresentar esses conceitos e iniciar o processo de familiarização das tecnologias empregadas.

lesson.description: O objetivo deste encontro é apresentar ao estudante os conceitos essenciais para o Processamento de Linguagem Natural. Quais são os conceitos principais e em quais áreas ele pode ser aplicado. Com o término da instrução, os estudantes deverão ser capazes de apresentar esses conceitos e iniciar o processo de familiarização das tecnologias empregadas.

repair_plan.explanation: The accepted/pruned balance suggests useful lesson-local concepts may have been discarded and need targeted re-evaluation.

target_candidates.label: Bash as Command Language Interpreter
target_candidates.description: Bash is a shell that interprets commands typed by the user to interact with the operating system.
coverage_criteria: Define Bash and explain its role as a command-language interpreter.
Identify that typing a command in the terminal and pressing enter causes the shell to interpret and execute that command.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: The video explicitly introduces Bash as a command language interpreter for interacting with the computer from the command line.
rationale.granularity_rationale: This is a foundational concept that can be verified by asking the student to define Bash or explain what happens when a command is entered.

target_candidates.label: Shell as Kernel Wrapper
target_candidates.description: The shell surrounds the operating system kernel, hiding its complexity and allowing programmers to execute tasks (data access, file creation) with simple commands.
coverage_criteria: Explain why the shell is considered a 'shell' around the kernel.
Describe how the shell simplifies access to system functionality like file management.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: The video describes the shell as 'surrounding the operating system kernel to hide its intricate details' and demonstrates basic commands like touch and cat.
rationale.granularity_rationale: The concept is small enough to be tested by asking the student to contrast the shell's role with the kernel's complexity.

target_candidates.label: History of Unix Shells
target_candidates.description: Unix shells evolved from the Thompson shell (1971) by Ken Thompson, to the Bourne shell by Stephen Bourne (1979), and finally to Bash (Bourne-Again Shell) by Brian Fox in 1989.
coverage_criteria: Name the three major shells in chronological order and their creators.
Explain why Bash is called the Bourne-Again Shell.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: The video provides a timeline of shell development, showing images and dates for Thompson, Bourne, and Bash.
rationale.granularity_rationale: This historical overview is a self-contained piece of knowledge that can be assessed with a few recall questions.

target_candidates.label: Bash as Default Unix Shell
target_candidates.description: On most Unix-like systems such as macOS and Linux distributions, Bash is the default shell when opening a terminal, providing a prompt for command input.
coverage_criteria: State that Bash is the default shell on many Unix systems.
Recognize the terminal prompt as the Bash shell waiting for commands.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: The video mentions that when you open the terminal on a Unix machine like macOS and most Linux distros, the default shell is usually Bash.
rationale.granularity_rationale: This fact can be verified with a simple yes/no or multiple-choice question, making it an appropriately granular candidate.

target_candidates.label: Checking Current Shell with `which $SHELL`
target_candidates.description: The command `which $SHELL` reveals the full path of the current shell executable (e.g., `/usr/bin/bash`), indicating whether Bash is running.
coverage_criteria: Execute `which $SHELL` in a terminal and interpret the output.
Explain that the shell is an application located in the binaries directory.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: The video demonstrates the command `which $SHELL` and its output `/usr/bin/bash` to verify that Bash is the running shell.
rationale.granularity_rationale: This is a single command that can be practiced and checked easily, representing a minimal checkable skill.

target_candidates.label: Bash as a Scripting Language
target_candidates.description: Bash is not only an interactive shell but also a programming language that allows writing scripts to automate command-line tasks.
coverage_criteria: Explain that Bash scripts automate sequences of commands.
Identify that a Bash script is a file containing bash commands that can be executed.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: The video states that Bash is also a programming language that allows us to write scripts, automating manual commands.
rationale.granularity_rationale: This concept distinguishes Bash's dual nature and can be assessed with a single explanation question.

target_candidates.label: Creating a Bash Script File
target_candidates.description: A Bash script is a plain text file (often with a `.sh` extension), starting with a shebang (`#!/usr/bin/bash`) that specifies the interpreter, followed by commands executed sequentially.
coverage_criteria: Write a script file with a shebang line and at least one command.
Explain the purpose of the shebang.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: The video demonstrates creating a script named beerme.sh, adding a shebang, and using echo, with the explanation that the first line should be the shebang followed by the path to the application.
rationale.granularity_rationale: This captures the minimal structure of a Bash script, which is a fundamental skill that can be tested with a short coding task.

target_candidates.label: Executing a Bash Script
target_candidates.description: A Bash script is run by typing its path, e.g., `./script.sh`, from the command line (assuming the file has execute permissions).
coverage_criteria: Execute a script located in the current directory using `./scriptname.sh`.
Explain that `./` refers to the current directory.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: The video runs the script by typing `./beerme.sh` into the shell, demonstrating the execution method.
rationale.granularity_rationale: This is a single operational step that can be verified by asking the student to run a given script.

target_candidates.label: Declaring and Using Variables in Bash
target_candidates.description: Variables in Bash are assigned with uppercase names and no spaces around `=` (e.g., `GREET="Hello"`) and are referenced by prefixing the name with `$` (e.g., `echo $GREET`).
coverage_criteria: Declare a variable in a Bash script.
Print the value of a variable using `$`.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: The video shows a variable `GREET="Howdy Partner"` and its use with `echo $GREET`, explicitly stating the rule: name in all caps, followed by equal sign, then reference with dollar sign.
rationale.granularity_rationale: Variable usage is a basic building block of scripting that can be validated with a simple exercise.

target_candidates.label: Using Positional Arguments ($1, $2, …)
target_candidates.description: When a script is invoked with arguments, those arguments are automatically available inside the script as $1, $2, etc., representing the first, second, etc. arguments.
coverage_criteria: Write a script that uses $1 and $2 to access passed arguments.
Explain that $0 typically contains the script name.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: The video demonstrates passing arguments `name age` and accessing them with `$1` and `$2` in the script.
rationale.granularity_rationale: Positional argument handling is a specific pattern in Bash scripting that can be assessed by having the student write or modify a script that uses them.

target_candidates.label: Conditional `if` Statements in Bash
target_candidates.description: Bash supports `if` statements with comparison operators (e.g., `-lt`, `-gt`, `-eq`); the syntax is `if [ condition ]; then ... else ... fi`.
coverage_criteria: Write an if statement that compares two numbers.
Explain the syntax of an if-fi block and the use of `-lt`.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: The video shows `if [ $2 -lt 21 ]; then echo "You are too young..." else fi` to implement conditional logic based on age.
rationale.granularity_rationale: Conditional logic is a fundamental programming construct; this candidate focuses specifically on its Bash syntax, making it a well-scoped checkable item.

target_candidates.label: User Input with `read` and Loops
target_candidates.description: The `read -p` command prompts for user input; constructs like `while true; do ... done` and `case` statements enable interactive looping and decision-making.
coverage_criteria: Write a script that repeatedly prompts the user using a while loop and read -p.
Use a case statement to branch on user responses, including options for yes/no.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: The video shows a script with `while true; do read -p ...; case $reply in [Yy]* ... esac; done` to ask for user confirmation.
rationale.granularity_rationale: This composite skill involves a few interrelated commands, still checkable with a focused coding exercise.

target_candidates.label: Bash Startup Files (.bash_profile and .bashrc)
target_candidates.description: When a Bash session starts, it automatically executes configuration files (typically `.bash_profile` or `.bashrc` in the home directory) to customize the shell environment.
coverage_criteria: Explain the purpose of startup scripts.
Identify that .bash_profile or .bashrc are used to set up aliases, environment variables, and prompt appearance.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: The video mentions that launching the shell runs a startup script defined in .bash_profile or .bashrc, and shows a customized prompt and git status as an example of customization.
rationale.granularity_rationale: This single configuration concept can be verified by asking where startup settings are stored and what they do.

target_candidates.label: Running Commands in the Background
target_candidates.description: Appending an ampersand (`&`) to a command runs it asynchronously in the background, allowing multiple long-running processes to run concurrently.
coverage_criteria: Demonstrate running a command in the background using `&`.
Explain that the shell prompt returns immediately while the command runs.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: The video shows multiple commands like `long_process &` to illustrate background execution, stating that adding an ampersand after a command runs it in the background.
rationale.granularity_rationale: This is a single shell feature that can be demonstrated with a short command, making it a concise checkable concept.

target_candidates.label: Google Colab as a cloud-based Python environment
target_candidates.description: Google Colab allows writing and executing Python code in the browser using Google's cloud infrastructure, based on Jupyter Notebooks. It supports real-time collaboration and eliminates local setup.
coverage_criteria: Can explain that Google Colab is a browser-based Python environment that uses notebooks.
Can demonstrate creating a new notebook and running a simple Python print command.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: The video explicitly introduces Google Colab as the recommended environment, showing the URL and how to create a new Python 3 notebook.
rationale.granularity_rationale: This is a single tool introduction, checkable by asking the student to describe or use the environment.

anchors: Creating a New Python Notebook in Colab

target_candidates.label: Python variable declaration without explicit keywords
target_candidates.description: In Python, variables are created by assignment without keywords like var, let, or const. Python uses implicit typing; the type is inferred from the assigned value.
coverage_criteria: Can correctly declare a string and integer variable in Python and print them.
Can explain that Python does not require explicit type declaration or var/let/const.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: The instructor demonstrates variable assignment nome = 'Michel' and idade = 37, and explicitly discusses the absence of declaration keywords compared to JavaScript.
rationale.granularity_rationale: This is a fundamental syntax rule, easily checkable with a simple coding exercise.

anchors: Python's Implicit Typing vs. JavaScript's Explicit Declaration

target_candidates.label: Defining functions with def, colon, and indentation
target_candidates.description: Python functions are defined using the def keyword followed by a name and parentheses. A colon indicates the start of the function body, which is delimited by consistent indentation (tabs or spaces), not curly braces.
coverage_criteria: Can write a function that takes a parameter and returns a value, using proper syntax and indentation.
Can explain that Python uses indentation to define blocks.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: The instructor explicitly teaches the def keyword, colons, and indentation by writing a function step-by-step and contrasting it with JavaScript syntax.
rationale.granularity_rationale: A core language construct; students can demonstrate it by writing a small function.

target_candidates.label: Notebook execution model: global scope and cell re-execution
target_candidates.description: In Jupyter/Colab notebooks, variables persist across cells in a global scope. Re-executing a cell updates its output but does not automatically re-execute other cells that may depend on it.
coverage_criteria: Can explain that a variable defined in one cell can be used in another cell.
Can identify the need to re-run dependent cells after a change.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: The instructor highlights that notebooks maintain a global scope and shows that re-executing a cell only affects its output, emphasizing the need to re-run related cells.
rationale.granularity_rationale: This is a specific operational concept about the notebook environment, distinct from Python syntax.

anchors: Basic Arithmetic Operations and Notebook Execution Flow

target_candidates.label: Python lists: creation, indexing, and negative indexing
target_candidates.description: Lists are ordered, mutable collections created with square brackets. Elements are accessed via zero-based index; negative indices access from the end (e.g., -1 for last element).
coverage_criteria: Can create a list with multiple items.
Can retrieve the first, last, and an inner element using positive and negative indices.
Can explain that indices start at 0.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: The instructor builds from separate variables to list creation, then demonstrates indexing with filmes[0], filmes[-1], and discusses IndexError for out-of-range.
rationale.granularity_rationale: This covers a specific data structure with its core operation; checkable via a short code task.

target_candidates.label: List slicing in Python
target_candidates.description: Slicing allows extracting a sublist using the colon operator: list[start:end]. Omitting start or end takes from the beginning or until the end. Negative indices can be used in slices.
coverage_criteria: Can slice a list to get elements from a specific index to the end.
Can explain that filmes[1:] returns all elements starting from index 1.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: The instructor explicitly shows filmes[1:] and filmes[-2:] and describes 'slicing and dicing' as a powerful feature.
rationale.granularity_rationale: Slicing is a distinct operation; a student can be asked to write a slice expression.

target_candidates.label: Iterating over lists with a for loop
target_candidates.description: Python's for loop iterates over the items of any iterable (like a list) using the syntax for item in iterable:. The loop body must be indented.
coverage_criteria: Can write a for loop that prints each element of a list.
Can explain the colon and indentation requirements.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: The instructor demonstrates a for loop over a film list, explaining the colon and indentation that define the loop body.
rationale.granularity_rationale: Basic control flow; checkable with a short loop task.

anchors: Iterating Through Lists with a `for` Loop

target_candidates.label: Python dictionaries: key-value storage
target_candidates.description: Dictionaries store key-value pairs using curly braces {}. Values are accessed by key using brackets, e.g., dados['nome']. They are analogous to objects in JavaScript or tables in Lua.
coverage_criteria: Can create a dictionary with at least two key-value pairs.
Can retrieve a value by its key.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: The instructor defines a dados dictionary and accesses nome and empresa keys, explicitly mentioning the key-value concept and comparing to JavaScript objects.
rationale.granularity_rationale: This introduces a distinct data structure; a student can demonstrate basic usage.

target_candidates.label: Python error messages: NameError and traceback interpretation
target_candidates.description: Python provides descriptive error messages like NameError when a variable or function name is not defined. The traceback shows the line number and file, aiding debugging.
coverage_criteria: Can identify a NameError in a traceback and explain that the name is misspelled or undefined.
Can correct a simple typo to resolve the error.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: The instructor intentionally triggers a NameError by misspelling a variable name and walks through the traceback to show how to locate the error.
rationale.granularity_rationale: This is a practical debugging skill; students can be asked to interpret an error message.

anchors: Combining Functions and Loops, and Handling Errors

target_candidates.label: f-string formatting in Python
target_candidates.description: Using f-strings (formatted string literals) to embed variables and expressions directly within string literals for output.
coverage_criteria: Student can write a print statement that includes a variable's value inside a string using an f-string (e.g., f"There are {count} items").
When asked, student can read an f-string and identify which parts are literal and which are evaluated expressions.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: Source explicitly explains f-strings as a 'special type of string to format' and demonstrates with code examples using variables like binary and do_not.
rationale.granularity_rationale: This is a concise, checkable language feature; understanding it can be tested with one or two simple coding tasks.

target_candidates.label: .format() string method
target_candidates.description: An alternative string formatting method in Python that uses the .format() syntax to substitute values into placeholders, often used when formatting an already-created string.
coverage_criteria: Student can convert an f-string to an equivalent .format() call.
Student can explain when .format() might be more useful than f-strings (e.g., format applied in a loop).

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: The source mentions .format() syntax on line 17 of the example and states it is used 'when I want to apply a format to an already created string, like in a loop.'
rationale.granularity_rationale: Limited to a single method of the string class; small enough to be described and demonstrated in a couple of questions.

target_candidates.label: Embedding variables in strings
target_candidates.description: The concept of inserting variable values into strings for output, distinguishing between literal text and dynamic data.
coverage_criteria: Student can verbally explain that strings can contain variables from the script.
Student can identify the parts of a formatted string that correspond to variables (e.g., {types_of_people}).

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: Source states 'strings can contain diverse variables that are in your script' and explains naming a variable and placing it inside a string.
rationale.granularity_rationale: A fundamental idea that underpins all string formatting; its understanding can be assessed with simple identification questions.

target_candidates.label: Command-line arguments with sys.argv
target_candidates.description: Using the sys module's argv list to receive arguments passed to a Python script from the command line.

current_reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: Both are annotation tasks applied to text after preprocessing; merging them provides a unified concept of linguistic annotation.
